newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian prosecutor appeals Alan Bond sentence.
newsitem.headline: Australian prosecutor appeals Alan Bond sentence.

text.p: Australia's chief prosecutor has lodged an appeal against the "manifestly inadequate" four-year sentence imposed on failed entrepreneur Alan Bond for the biggest corporate fraud in Australian history.
"An appeal has been lodged on the inadequacy of the sentence imposed on Alan Bond," a spokesman for the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions told Reuters on Tuesday.
The prosecution in Bond's A$1.0 billion (US$776 million) fraud trial in Perth earlier this month had asked the judge to hand down the maximum sentence of 10 years.

But the judge shocked the Australian legal community when he sentenced Bond to serve only four years jail and made the sentence concurrent with Bond's current jail term, enabling him to be free on parole from 1998 after serving a minimum one-year non-parole period.
"The total sentence was manifestly inadequate in all the circumstances in the case," according to the appeal document lodged with the Western Australia Supreme Court.
The appeal said the four-year jail sentence failed to reflect the "total criminality of the conduct" and failed to reflect general deterrence for such a crime.
It also said the judge gave "undue weight" to Alan Bond's personal matters and that the judge erred in allowing the sentence to be served concurrently.

In handing down his sentence, the judge noted mitigating circumstances included Bond's age, his substantial contribution to the community, his offer to co-operate in other cases, the humiliation of conviction and his early pleas of guilty.
Bond, 58, already serving a three-year sentence for an earlier fraud involving the French impressionist painting La Promenade, pleaded guilty to two charges of dishonesty last December.

Bond admitted that in 1988 and 1989 he failed to act honestly as a company director and acted with intent to defraud when he created a A$1.0 billion unsecured loan from Bell Resources to his ailing Bond Corp.
